title: KV-aware merge arbiter: token-vs-request fairness sketch
body:
Context and motivation:

This is a working sketch exploring a middle ground between strictly request-level and strictly token-level continuous batching. The goal is to get the unit-cost benefits of token coalescing while avoiding long-tail latency degradation for small, latency-sensitive requests and preserving KV cache locality for multi-turn chats. Existing sketches in the folder focus heavily on windowing and continuous coalescers; here I want to center the design on an arbiter that merges inputs across two axes: KV affinity and latency credits (micro-deadlines).

High-level goals (non-exhaustive):
- Preserve KV cache affinity for active chat sessions so that hot KV lookups remain local to the same slab/kernel and do not suffer expensive re-materialization.
- Avoid head-of-line blocking for low-token requests (e.g., 1–8 tokens) from high-priority tenants.
- Realize most of continuous batching economics: maintain high average batch fill for kernels, particularly for large-seq models.
- Be implementable as a relatively small arbiter layer on top of existing microbatching/merge pipeline (minimal kernel changes).
- Provide clear telemetry hooks: per-tenant latency SLO attainment, cache-hit rates, kernel occupancy.

Key constraints and observed workload patterns:
- Many requests are short: single-shot completion or short chat turns. But a small fraction of long decodes dominate GPU time.
- KV cache affinity matters: repeated chat turns from same session often reuse keys; breaking affinity increases memory churn and kernel warmup cost.
- Kernel shapes differ: some kernels are optimized for seq<=128, others for longer; merging should consider kernel compatibility.
- We must keep scheduling decisions cheap—O(1) or O(log n) per arrival.

Core idea: KV-aware merge arbiter with priority lanes and micro-deadlines

Design components:
1) Request descriptor (metadata per incoming request)
   - tenant_id, session_id (if present), preferred_kernel_hint (from compiler), estimated_remaining_tokens (if available), requested_priority (api/plan), arrival_ts.
   - KV-hotness score: computed as cache.get_estimated_session_hit_rate(session_id) or fallback heuristics (recent-turn-counts for session).

2) Two-tier buffer model per worker (or per kernel-group):
   - affinity lanes: hashed by (tenant_id, session_id) coalesced into a small set of affinity buckets. Each bucket holds pending partial decodes that share KV. This keeps potential coalesces local.
   - opportunistic pool: any request that does not declare strong KV affinity lands here and can be merged widely for max fill.

3) Micro-deadlines / latency credits
   - On arrival, each request gets a micro-deadline = arrival_ts + base_slo_budget, where base_slo_budget is a small tunable (e.g., 8–25ms depending on plan). Additionally, high-priority requests get boosted credits (smaller budgets).
   - The arbiter keeps a min-heap keyed by micro-deadline. When a micro-deadline expires, the corresponding lane/pool gets flushed (merged) even if below ideal fill.

4) Merge policy (when to form a kernel batch)
   - Preferred path: join items inside same affinity bucket first (if kernel compatibility allows). This preserves KV locality and increases likelihood of cache hits.
   - If an affinity bucket cannot reach a target fill within half of micro-deadline, allow it to pull low-KV-affinity items from opportunistic pool up to kernel compatibility constraints (sequence length, dtype/quantization flag, compile-time kernel hints).
   - If a micro-deadline triggers, flush with whatever is available after attempting the minimal affinity-preserving merges.
   - To avoid starvation of opportunistic items, occasionally (configurable fraction) force affinity buckets to relinquish a slot for global-merge candidates when the opportunistic pool has many waiting items and kernel occupancy is low.

5) Kernel compatibility filter
   - Each candidate pinned for a kernel batch must satisfy kernel hints. We maintain small precomputed compatibility masks per request descriptor to keep checks cheap.
   - If no single kernel can cover all candidates, batch splits by kernel group preserving affinity order as much as possible.

6) KV cache affinity heuristics
   - Affinity buckets are size-limited: if a single bucket accumulates too many waiting tokens and would cause large delays to others in same bucket, we split it (approx LRU split) to maintain fairness across sessions.
   - For ephemeral sessions (single-turn), KV-hotness=low; they default to opportunistic pool.

Fairness reasoning (token vs request)

This arbiter blends both notions:
- Token-level economic goals are achieved by opportunistic merging and permissive pulls into affinity buckets when beneficial. In steady-state high load, the opportunistic pool drives kernel fill and amortizes per-token cost.
- Request-level fairness is preserved via micro-deadlines and priority lanes: short requests will not be indefinitely delayed because their credits expire and force flushes. Tenants with explicit higher priority or lower budget can be configured with narrower deadlines (service tiers).

Edge cases and mitigation:
- Priority inversion: a high-priority small request stuck behind a large affinity bucket. Mitigation: allow preemption of one slot in affinity flush when micro-deadline of a high-priority request is nearing expiry. Implementation: marking one candidate as preemptible and replacing it with the high-priority item; evicted item moves back to opportunistic pool with adjusted micro-deadline.
- Cache thrash: aggressively merging across sessions might cause cache eviction churn. Mitigation: track per-kernel cache miss penalty estimate and bias merges toward affinity when cost model predicts net savings.
- Kernel underutilization due to incompatible hints: add a fallback slower kernel that is compatible with many shapes for low-latency flushes (falling back to slightly higher cost to meet latency SLOs).

Telemetry and SLO signals to expose:
- per-session cache-hit-rate (pre/post-merge), average kernel utilization, average batch fill, 50/95/99 latency by request-size bucket, number of preemptions, opportunistic-pool wait time distribution, eviction counts from affinity buckets.

Experiment plan (A/B phases):
- Phase 0: Simulate with production trace (1 week) to tune micro-deadline defaults and pull thresholds; offline cost model estimation for cache-miss penalty.
- Phase 1: Canary on one worker-pool (low-risk model) with telemetry only (no auto preemption). Compare cost per token and p95 latency for small requests.
- Phase 2: Enable preemption and dynamic pulls for a subset of tenants (opt-in). Observe fairness metrics.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is the best default micro-deadline per plan? Workload dependent — propose initial defaults: free-tier 20ms, standard 15ms, enterprise 8ms. Need trace-driven tuning.
- Cost model for cache eviction: need to instrument kernel warmup times and memory writeback cost.
- How to encode session affinity securely for Private deployments where session ids cannot leave customer boundary? Likely handled by worker-local hashing; ensure no cross-tenant leakage.
- Race conditions when splitting affinity buckets during flush; need lock-free enqueue/dequeue scheme or tiny spinlocks.
- Backpressure to API layer: when opportunistic pool grows, consider returning early 429s for low-priority clients.

Notes to implementer:
- Focus arbiter as a thin, mostly stateless decision layer; keep per-request descriptor compact.
- Reuse existing continuous-batcher APIs where possible; implement affinity buckets as additional queueing layer in front of merge.
- Add kernel-compatibility bitsets to request descriptors at admission to avoid heavy checks during merge.

References/links:
- GH PR: runtime/pull/912 (batching infra changes)
- Ticket: RUNTIME-734 (kv cache instrumentation)
- Slack threads: #serving-runtime for prior conversations (see pinned message on 2025-01-20)

Conclusion (short):
This sketch attempts to balance token-level efficiency and request-level fairness while preserving KV cache locality that is crucial for multi-turn chat performance. If the team likes the direction, next steps are: simulate on traces, add lightweight cost estimator for cache penalty, and prototype arbiter with telemetry-only canary.

Quick TODO (assign):
- Ava: run trace simulation and produce tuning table (by 2025-03-09)
- Marco: prototype micro-deadline min-heap and affinity buckets in batching service (POC by 2025-03-16)
- Priya: define telemetry dashboards and cost model inputs (by 2025-03-12)
- Jon: review kernel compatibility bitset API and add flags to compiler output (PR draft by 2025-03-10)

Unresolved: is 'opportunistic pull' worth the extra complexity if most traffic is single-turn? Simulation will tell.
